real.title: What if my problems are real?
real.description: This article explores the difference between depression and natural sadness, highlighting that depression is linked to cognitive distortions, whereas sadness is a normal response to life events. It explains that even serious challenges do not lead directly to depression; instead, they affect our emotional state through the filter of our thoughts. Understanding and addressing unhelpful thoughts can significantly help in managing depression, distinguishing it from the natural sadness caused by life circumstances.

texts: While reading our section on depression or studying the cognitive approach to this disorder, you might wonder: “CBT suggests that depression is linked to cognitive distortions, but what if my problems are real?”.
You might feel that your “realistic” problems—such as the death of a loved one, financial struggles, debt, bankruptcy, or illness—lead to a “realistic depression.”.
We aren’t dismissing any of these hardships; we certainly aren’t. However, these problems are not the cause of a “realistic depression.” In fact, such a thing doesn’t exist!
Sometimes we label things as depression when they aren’t, confusing the disorder with melancholy, sadness, or periods of low mood.
While these negative emotions are part of depressive disorders, there are significant differences between them.
<q author="Dan Reynolds">People who have never experienced depression think it’s just sadness or a bad mood. For me, it’s not depression; it’s falling into a state of grayness and numbness.</q>
The core question lies in defining the boundary between normal sadness and depression. What is the difference between “helpful sadness” and true depression?
<important>Sadness is a natural emotion that arises in response to a realistic awareness of a negative event involving loss or disappointment.</important>
For example, when we lose a loved one, we rightfully feel that life will be difficult and painful without them.
These feelings are natural, justified, and even meaningful, as they make us deeper and add meaning to our lives. In this way, loss can bring us much.
Depression is a disorder that is driven by cognitive distortions.

For instance, if in a similar situation we start telling ourselves, “I’ll never be happy again because they died. It’s not fair!”—such thoughts trigger feelings of self-pity and despair. These emotions, rooted in distortions, are what ultimately weigh us down.
Following a loss, illness, breakup, divorce, or a major setback, we may experience either depression or sadness.
However, sadness is not distorted.
It is simply the result of a natural emotional flow and is, therefore, temporary. Sadness is not linked to a loss of self-esteem.

Depression is more persistent, and its symptoms can intensify. It lasts for most of every day for at least two consecutive weeks. Nothing can distract you from dark thoughts, nothing brings joy, and life feels colorless. And it is always linked to a loss of self-esteem.
Depression that arises following an obvious stressor is sometimes called “reactive” depression.

test.question: Which symptoms characterize depression as opposed to natural sadness?
answers: Short-term feelings of sadness following an unpleasant event
A temporary loss of interest in favorite activities
A prolonged state of apathy and despair
Increased feelings of energy and activity

texts: However, it can sometimes be difficult to identify a specific stressful event that triggered the episode. Such depression is often called “endogenous,” as it seems like the symptoms arise from nowhere.
But in both cases, the underlying cause of depression is the same: unhelpful, negative thoughts.
<important>Depression serves no adaptive or productive function and is one of the most severe forms of suffering.</important>
The only positive side is the growth you may experience by working through it.
If depression begins after a specific event, that event is merely a trigger, not the sole cause of the disorder.
The psyche has already been altered; it only required a small impulse to set the mechanism in motion.
When something truly difficult happens in your life, your emotional state is heavily influenced by your thoughts and how you perceive the situation.

rebuff.title: Technique: Stand Up to Your Inner Critic
rebuff.description: This article presents effective self-help methods for boosting self-esteem. The core technique involves learning to challenge your inner critic by keeping a specialized record of self-critical thoughts, their cognitive distortions, and adaptive responses. The article emphasizes the importance of regular practice to achieve significant changes in self-perception and improve self-esteem.

texts: We’ve developed a series of simple yet effective techniques to help boost your self-esteem. These methods are designed for self-help and will support you through this challenging process.
First and foremost, it’s important to understand: simply knowing the theory isn’t enough to improve your self-esteem.
Only regular practice will bring lasting results. We recommend dedicating a little time to this every day—at least in the beginning, until it becomes a habit.
The first technique we’d like to introduce is designed to help you learn how to stand up to your inner critic.
<activitylink id="DzseWuFv2t">
Feelings of inadequacy and self-hatred often stem from an inner critic that constantly undermines your self-esteem.
Unhelpful beliefs like “I’m worthless,” “I’m worse than others,” “I’ll never succeed,” “Everything is my fault,” or “I’m a failure” worsen self-esteem issues and can lead to depression.
To break this negative thinking habit, follow this plan:
• Learn to notice and record your self-critical thoughts.
• Identify the cognitive distortions in those thoughts.
• Develop adaptive responses to create a more realistic and helpful relationship with yourself, and do this regularly.
You can use the “Automatic Thought Journal” in our app for this, or you can keep track of them outside the app using a three-column format.
To keep things simple, we’ll explain the process using the three-column method.
<q author="Eleanor Roosevelt">No one can make you feel inferior without your consent.</q>
Create a three-column table in whatever format works best for you—a notebook, a computer document, or a note on your phone. Label the columns:
• Critic’s thoughts
• Cognitive distortion
• Adaptive response
In the first column, write down every self-critical thought that comes to mind.
<important>Every time you blame yourself, feel useless, or feel dissatisfied with yourself, ask: “What am I thinking about myself right now?” and write it down.</important>
For example, if you’re feeling anxious before an exam and think, “I’m so stupid, I’m definitely going to fail,” that is exactly the kind of thought you need to record.
In this column, you should write down your actual thoughts about yourself, not your feelings. If you write, “I feel terrible,” it will be hard to challenge because that is, in fact, how you feel.
In the second column, identify which cognitive distortion is present in the thought.
Write down the cognitive distortion you’ve identified. It might be just one, or it could be two or even three.
For instance, in the statement “I’m so stupid, I’m definitely going to fail,” we see the distortion of labeling.
In the thought “I’m incapable of anything, so I’ll get expelled and never succeed,” you might find several distortions, such as overgeneralization and catastrophizing.
<q author="Carl Rogers">The better I understand myself and my emotional needs, the stronger my perception of reality becomes, and the fewer fears and delusions poison my life.</q>
And of course, the most important column in our table is the adaptive response. This is where you truly stand up to your inner critic.
It’s important to replace self-critical thoughts with more realistic and logical ones, while avoiding overly optimistic statements.
You need to replace the critical thought with something more realistic. Avoid being dichotomous by replacing it with an overly optimistic thought that doesn’t feel true.

<important>Avoid thoughts like, “I’m the smartest person here and I’ll ace everything.” While that might turn out to be true, it’s the polar opposite of your original thought and you’re unlikely to believe it right away—which means it won’t be helpful.</important>
Instead, try to find the truth—how things actually are.
Because if what you write as your adaptive response doesn’t feel convincing and realistic to you, it won’t help.
Try to write an adaptive response that you actually believe.

For example, you might write: “I’m not actually stupid; I have evidence to prove it. I got into university on my own and I’m doing well enough. Of course, there are moments when I struggle, but I’m only human and I can make mistakes—that doesn’t make me stupid.”

“Besides, I’m preparing for my exam and I’ll most likely pass it with at least a passing grade, as I’ve passed all my other subjects before. And even if I don’t pass on the first try, I can retake it, prepare better, and make sure I pass next time.”
Such an adaptive response is more plausible, and you are much more likely to believe it.
Use this tool throughout the day, regularly recording your thoughts and challenging unhelpful beliefs.
Over time, you’ll find that finding an adaptive response becomes easier. But most importantly, you’ll notice changes in your mood and how you feel about yourself.

self_help.title: Through the Dark Days: Self-Help as a Path out of Depression
self_help.description: This article explores the many facets of depression and offers a clear look at evidence-based treatments—including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and bibliotherapy—supported by research findings. It aims to equip readers with practical self-help tools and grounded hope for recovery, even in severe cases.

texts: Depression is like a dark veil covering the souls and minds of many of us. Each year, this mental health disorder becomes more prevalent, invisibly weaving itself into people’s lives and leaving behind exhaustion, a loss of interest, pessimistic thoughts, feelings of alienation, sadness about the past, and anxiety about the future. It can feel as though it is pulling a person into a world without joy or light.

If these words resonate with you, you have likely experienced depression personally or through loved ones. The disorder is so common that it is sometimes compared to the “common cold” of mental health. Depression is a modern-day epidemic that strips life of its meaning and joy, sometimes even threatening life itself.
However, not every sad moment means depression. In the following chapters, we will explore how to recognize that fine line.

Let’s start with a definition. Depression (from the Latin depressio, meaning to depress or lower) is a mental health disorder described by the World Health Organization as a state of despondency, loss of interest and pleasure, feelings of guilt or low self-esteem, sleep and appetite disturbances, fatigue, and concentration problems.

<q author="Aaron Beck">Depression is a “multifaceted” disorder; it can be “smiling,” masking itself as an organic illness, while organic disorders, in turn, can dress themselves in the clothes of depression.</q>

It sounds grim, but there is good news: depression is treatable. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a reliable and effective approach to managing this condition. By mastering it, you can learn to shift your mood and manage your symptoms on your own.

Numerous studies confirm the effectiveness of CBT. However, we also want to emphasize the importance of self-help, which plays a key role in the recovery process, whether or not you are receiving professional treatment.

<important>For example, research by Dr. Forrest Scogin and his colleagues at the University of Alabama showed that bibliotherapy—therapy through reading a good self-help book—can be as effective as traditional treatment.</important>
In their experiment, participants who read David Burns’ “Feeling Good” (Mood Therapy) showed significant improvements comparable to the effects of full psychotherapy or antidepressant medication.
In this unique study, Dr. Forrest Scogin and his colleague Dr. Christine Jamison brought new insight to the treatment of depression.

They divided participants suffering from severe depression into two groups. The first group, called the “Immediate Bibliotherapy Group,” was offered David Burns’ “Feeling Good” to read over a period of four weeks.
The second group, named the “Delayed Bibliotherapy Group,” was placed on a waiting list for treatment, waiting for their turn during the first month of the experiment.
The patients in the “Delayed Bibliotherapy Group” served as a control group, ensuring that the improvements in the “Immediate Bibliotherapy Group” were not simply due to the passage of time.

Before the study began, all patients were asked to take two tests. The first was the Beck Depression Inventory, a time-tested self-assessment test that patients complete on their own. The second was the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, which is completed alongside trained depression researchers.

After four weeks, the results for both groups were reassessed. Significant improvement was observed in the “Immediate Bibliotherapy Group”: the average scores on the Beck and Hamilton scales dropped to 10 or below, indicating a normalization of their condition.
The data showed not only significant improvement in condition but also an absence of relapse for three months following the experiment, with results continuing to improve.

At the same time, the scores in the “Delayed Bibliotherapy Group” remained unchanged, proving that the improvements in the first group were not just a result of time passing. Once the second group was also provided with the book, their condition improved in a similar way.
Thus, the study demonstrates the significant potential of self-help in combating depression. The improvements were so noticeable that most study participants did not require further treatment.
This was one of the first studies to confirm the effectiveness of self-help in treating depression, but it was far from the only one.

It is also worth noting research by Scottish scientists, which opened a new chapter in understanding depression treatment. They found that self-help books can be unexpectedly effective in fighting this disorder.
These findings were based on a carefully planned experiment involving more than 200 people suffering from mild to moderate depression.

Participants in the study were divided into two groups, each receiving different treatments over several months. The first group relied solely on antidepressants, while the second immersed themselves in the world of bibliotherapy.
As it turned out, participants in the group that turned to specialized reading demonstrated significantly more impressive recovery results than those who were limited to taking antidepressants.
The inspiring studies that scientists used as a foundation for therapy were built on the fundamental principles of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).
<important>This self-help phenomenon, as it turns out, plays a key role in the journey to overcoming depression. It was this very thought that inspired us to create this section.</important>
We want to give you the key to understanding what is happening in your life and offer tools that you can use to manage it on your own.
Step by step, we will share important information about depression with you, providing powerful tools and techniques that will help you acquire the necessary skills to manage things yourself.
As a result, you will gain the skills to find the strength to emerge from the deadlock of painful emotions.

Remember that after every storm comes a calm, the sky clears, and the sun rises again to light up everything around you. In those moments, feelings of joy and relief emerge, along with an irrepressible desire to live that is incomparable to anything else.
If you are struggling with depression right now, remember: change is not only possible, it is inevitable with the right approach, no matter how heavy and hopeless your current circumstances may seem.
